items.prompt: Why does updateTicket run canEditTicket BEFORE the tenant-scoped findFirst rather than after it?
items.answer: Gating first returns 403 with no query, so a viewer cannot tell a 404 from a 403
distractors: findFirst needs the caller's role to choose which include shape to load for the ticket
Prisma refuses to run queries for a role that carries no write permission at all
Order does not matter for safety, and the gate was moved first only for the unit test
items.explanation: The role gate is the first line of the service (ticketService.ts:172-174), so a viewer PATCH stops before the lookup at :176 and before the 404 at :181 could disclose anything.

items.prompt: An AGENT of tenant A sends a valid ticket id that belongs to tenant B. What status comes back, and why that one?
items.answer: 404: the lookup filters by id and tenantId, so a foreign id looks like a missing one
distractors: 403: the service detects that the ticket belongs to another tenant and refuses explicitly
200: the AGENT role may edit any ticket by id, so the update goes through normally
500: PostgreSQL row-level security raises an error that the middleware does not map
items.explanation: `where: { id, tenantId: auth.tenantId }` - the schema has no row-level security; the service predicate is the only thing selecting the right tenant.

items.prompt: A VIEWER (rather than an agent) PATCHes the same foreign-tenant ticket id. What do they get?
items.answer: 403 from the role gate, before any tenant lookup runs
distractors: 404, the same as the agent, because tenant scope is checked before the role
200 with the ticket, but with its public comments only
401 for the foreign tenant, as no session covers it
items.explanation: Trace D: canEditTicket("VIEWER") is false, so the request never reaches the tenant-scoped findFirst.

items.prompt: Before the repair, GET hid an internal note from a viewer but PATCH returned it. What general rule does the fix encode?
items.answer: Every endpoint returning a ticket is a read path, so both share one role-aware include
distractors: Write endpoints should never return the updated resource, only a status code and an id
Comment filtering belongs in the client, which already knows the signed-in viewer's role
Internal notes belong in a separate table that a PATCH response can never join against
items.explanation: getTicket filtered comments inline while updateTicket used the unfiltered ticketInclude; one shared helper means the two paths cannot drift again.

items.prompt: The outbox insert fails after the ticket update inside updateTicket's transaction. What does the client see, and does the audit row exist?
items.answer: A 500 and no audit row, since all three writes commit together or not at all
distractors: A 200, because the ticket update succeeded and the outbox insert is best-effort
A 500, but the audit row remains because it was inserted before any outbox row
A 409 mapped from the Prisma error, with the ticket update always kept in place
items.explanation: All three writes are in one prisma.$transaction callback; the Prisma error is not an HttpError, so errorMiddleware answers 500. A rolled-back change can never have announced itself.

items.prompt: withSerializableRetry re-runs the callback on Prisma P2034 only. Why NOT also retry an HttpError or a P2002?
items.answer: An HttpError is a decision and a P2002 will recur, but a P2034 can pass on retry
distractors: Retrying those errors would exhaust Prisma's connection pool under load, so they are passed through
They are retried as well, just later, by Express's error middleware rather than inside the wrapper
P2002 and HttpError are thrown outside the transaction callback, so the wrapper can never catch them
items.explanation: Serializable means retry or it means nothing: SQLSTATE 40001 (Prisma P2034) is PostgreSQL asking the app to retry; everything else passes through untouched.

items.prompt: Agents A and B both read a NEW ticket; A sets RESOLVED and B sets PENDING. A commits first. Why does Serializable isolation not stop B from writing PENDING over RESOLVED?
items.answer: The read and transition check run before the transaction opens, so it has nothing to guard
distractors: It does stop it: PostgreSQL raises 40001 and the retry re-validates the transition from the fresh state
RESOLVED to PENDING is a legal transition in the table, so there is nothing that needs to be stopped
Serializable isolation only applies to inserts, and this transaction performs an update on the ticket
items.explanation: Even a 40001 retry re-runs only the callback, which repeats the unvalidated update. The fix is to move the read and assertTicketTransition inside the transaction (or predicate the update on the expected status).

items.prompt: An AGENT sends { status: CLOSED } on an OPEN ticket. What is the response, and why is it arguably a bug?
items.answer: 500: agents may close only from RESOLVED or PENDING, and the plain Error is unmapped
distractors: 403, because the domain rule refuses agents and is mapped to an HttpError by the service
200: agents can close from any state; only viewers are refused by the transition table
409: the conventional status the middleware assigns to every invalid transition
items.explanation: A client mistake reported as a server error. The suggested fix keeps HTTP out of the domain: export a TicketTransitionError and map it to 409 in errorMiddleware.

items.prompt: An OPEN ticket has exactly 0 ms left before its SLA deadline. What does getSlaState return?
distractors: BREACHED
MET
PAUSED
items.explanation: Only a negative remainder is BREACHED; the last hour is inclusive at both 60 minutes and zero: `if (msRemaining < 0) return BREACHED; if (msRemaining <= 60 * 60_000) return AT_RISK;`

items.prompt: A HIGH ticket due at 17:00 sits in PENDING until 18:00 and is then reopened. What SLA state does it show right after reopening?
items.answer: BREACHED: PAUSED was just a label, and the stored slaDueAt did not move
distractors: MET: the hour spent in PENDING is credited back to the stored deadline
AT_RISK: reopening a ticket restarts the final-hour warning window
PAUSED, until an agent posts the first reply after the ticket reopens
items.explanation: SLA state is derived, not stored; truly pausing needs a stored pause start or accumulated paused time that pushes slaDueAt forward on leaving PENDING.

items.prompt: An URGENT ticket is minutes from breaching. An agent sets it to LOW and then back to URGENT. What happens to the SLA?
items.answer: It gets a fresh two hours, because every priority change recomputes slaDueAt from now
distractors: Nothing changes: slaDueAt is computed from createdAt, so priority churn cannot move it
It breaches immediately, because the LOW step always counts as an SLA downgrade
The second change is refused, because priority changes are rate-limited per ticket
items.explanation: `slaDueAt: priority changed ? calculateSlaDueAt(new Date(), priority) : undefined` - finding F5 calls this an SLA clock reset.

items.prompt: A read-only VIEWER posts a PUBLIC reply on a ticket nobody has answered yet. What side effects follow?
items.answer: It sets firstResponseAt and then notifies the customer
distractors: None: viewers cannot comment, so the post is refused
The comment is saved but hidden until an agent approves it
It is stored as INTERNAL automatically, so nobody is notified
items.explanation: addTicketComment only blocks INTERNAL notes for viewers; a PUBLIC reply from anyone sets firstResponseAt when it is still null (finding F6).

items.front: authMiddleware picks the user from x-tenant-slug and x-user-email headers, defaulting to seeded values (auth.ts:20-26). Why is this a deployment blocker?
items.back: Identity is asserted, not proved: any caller who knows an admin's email becomes that admin, and a request with no headers is agent@acme.test. Put a session or token check in front of authMiddleware; everything after it can stay.

items.front: The outbox worker selects PENDING rows, then marks each PROCESSING in a separate statement (worker.ts:7-25). What breaks at scale and how do you fix it?
items.back: Two workers take the same batch and deliver twice; a crash mid-row leaves it PROCESSING forever; FAILED rows are never retried and attempts has no limit. Claim with UPDATE ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED and add a lease timeout.

items.front: POST /api/notifications/inbound-email creates tickets directly in the route (notificationRoutes.ts:16-30). List what it bypasses.
items.back: No role gate (viewers can create tickets), no audit row, an unretried ticket-number race at default isolation, and no idempotency: a redelivered email hits the externalId unique constraint and returns 500. Route it through a service that looks up externalId first and reuses createTicket's numbering and retry.

items.front: canTransitionTicket returns true for same-status moves before it checks for VIEWER (index.ts:33-34). Why does it matter if updateTicket already blocks viewers?
items.back: It is latent: any new caller that relies on the domain function alone inherits a viewer no-op that passes. Order domain checks so role refusal comes before shortcuts, so the domain rule is safe on its own.
